3.4.2.1-f1.accuracy_reason: In Juvenal 2.152 the bath fee is the quadrans, and small children went in free.

3.4.2.1-f11.accuracy_reason: Suetonius, Nero 38, reports the Greek line 'emou thanontos…' and Nero's reply 'emou zontos'.

3.4.2.1-f122.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.61 ('nil conscire sibi, nulla pallescere culpa') praises a clear conscience; Burton uses it of men who feel no guilt at all.

3.4.2.1-f131.accuracy_reason: Amores 3.9.35–36, the elegy on Tibullus, begins 'Cum rapiunt mala fata bonos'.

3.4.2.1-f135.accuracy_reason: In Contra Celsum 3.34 and following, Celsus sets Zalmoxis, Mopsus, Amphiaraus, Trophonius and others beside Christ.

3.4.2.1-f136.accuracy_reason: Giordano Bruno was burned in Rome in February 1600, and 'infelix' does carry the sense 'ill-fated'.

3.4.2.1-f14.accuracy_reason: The couplet 'Nocte pluit tota…' is attributed to Virgil in the Donatus Life of Virgil.

3.4.2.1-f142.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Consolation 1 prose 4 has 'Si quidem deus est, unde mala? bona vero unde, si non est?', and Cotta argues the point in De natura deorum book 3.

3.4.2.1-f16.accuracy_reason: Germania 46 on the Fenni is quoted correctly. Burton does reverse the order of the clauses and shorten the wording.

3.4.2.1-f17.accuracy_reason: This is Aeneid 6.471, on Dido's shade unmoved by Aeneas. Marpessos is indeed the marble mountain on Paros.

3.4.2.1-f18.accuracy_reason: The proverb appears in Terence, Phormio 186 ('laterem lavem'), and in Erasmus's Adagia ('Laterem lavas').

3.4.2.1-f19.accuracy_reason: The source is Tacitus, Annals 16.19. Tacitus's text has no 'amicos' and reads 'sapientium', so both claims about Burton's changes are right.

3.4.2.1-f20.accuracy_reason: These are Peter's words in Matthew 17:4, and the Vulgate does read 'bonum est nos hic esse'.

3.4.2.1-f28.accuracy_reason: Caecilius says this in Octavius 12, and Burton's wording is indeed loose.

3.4.2.1-f3.accuracy_reason: In Euripides' Cyclops (lines 334–335), Polyphemus sacrifices only to himself and to his belly, 'greatest of the gods'.

3.4.2.1-f31.accuracy_reason: Modern editions number this Martial 4.21 and name the man Segius. Burton's sidenote cites it as 1.21.

3.4.2.1-f32.accuracy_reason: In Octavius 12.2 the passage is longer ('ut dicitis, egetis, algetis, operibus et fame laboratis…'), so Burton has abridged it.

3.4.2.1-f36.accuracy_reason: The English gloss does echo Acts 26:24, and the Vulgate of Romans 11:20 does read 'noli altum sapere'.

3.4.2.1-f54.accuracy_reason: 'Semper paret, semel iussit' is from De Providentia 5.8. The note links the rest to Naturales Quaestiones 2.35 with a hedge ('echoes'); Burton's sidenote cites chapters 33 and 36 of the same book.

3.4.2.1-f56.accuracy_reason: Peregrinus 13 calls Christ 'that crucified sophist' (τὸν ἀνεσκολοπισμένον ἐκεῖνον σοφιστήν). In ch. 11 he is 'the man crucified in Palestine', so Lucian never calls him a god.

3.4.2.1-f58.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 1.62–65 praises Epicurus, and 'religio' there means fear of the gods, or superstition.

3.4.2.1-f59.accuracy_reason: Pliny, Natural History 7.188 (book 7, chapter 55 in older editions) reads 'omnibus a supremo die eadem quae ante primum'. The sidenote paraphrases this.

3.4.2.1-f60.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Letters 54.4 reads 'hoc erit post me quod ante me fuit'. The note rightly records that Burton has 'Idem' for 'hoc' and cites an older numbering.

3.4.2.1-f61.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Letters 54.5 compares a lamp after it is put out with the lamp before it was lit. The note rightly calls Burton's sentence a paraphrase.

3.4.2.1-f65.accuracy_reason: The three-rings parable is Decameron 1.3. The claim about where the Latin wording comes from is suitably hedged.

3.4.2.1-f66.accuracy_reason: De tribus impostoribus was a legendary book that was rumoured more than seen, and the Cymbalum mundi is by Bonaventure des Périers. 'Inquit' most plausibly refers to Mersenne, whom Burton names just before.

3.4.2.1-f74.accuracy_reason: Erasmus does collect 'Omnium horarum homo' in the Adagia (1.3.86), for a man suited to every occasion and company.

3.4.2.1-f76.accuracy_reason: Persius 2.17–18 reads 'heus age, responde (minimum est quod scire laboro) / de Iove quid sentis?'. The note describes Burton's changes correctly.

3.4.2.1-f78.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.21–22 is about an unbaked pot: 'sonat vitium percussa, maligne / respondet'. The account of Burton's changes is correct, and the biblical echo is fairly hedged.

3.4.2.1-f83.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.16.45 reads 'introrsum turpem, speciosum pelle decora', in the singular.

3.4.2.1-f86.accuracy_reason: Romans 2:5 in the Vulgate reads 'thesaurizas tibi iram in die irae'.

3.4.2.1-f97.accuracy_reason: Genius was a person's guardian spirit, and 'genio indulgere' is a standard Latin idiom for indulging oneself.
